evidence_set: To check duration, baseline-corrected scores of the five general drug-effect items were examined at 6 and 8 h: no MDMA effect was significantly elevated at 6 h, while MDA raised all five at 6 h and all except bad drug effect at 8 h. At 6 h any drug effect was 41.6 ± 7 points higher after MDA than after MDMA (z = 6.3, p < 0.001) and 46.4 ± 7 higher than its placebo (z = 6.7, p < 0.001); at 8 h it was 35.6 ± 10 above placebo (t = 3.7, p = 0.001). No MDMA values are shown at 8 h in Figure 2 (the methods state a 6-h limit for the MDMA data only for heart rate and blood pressure), so the 8-h comparison is with placebo only.

Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (66 items), given 8 h after dosing for retrospective peak ratings, N = 12 per drug, F(3,21): MDA > MDMA (both > placebo) on complex imagery 20.6, elementary imagery 13.9 and spiritual experience 24.8; MDMA > MDA and MDMA > placebo on dread of ego dissolution 15.1, impaired control and cognition 11.1 and anxiety 5.09 (p = 0.008), with no significant MDA–placebo difference listed; audio-visual synesthesia 8.26, with MDA > placebo the only listed difference; both drugs above placebo on oceanic boundlessness 35.9, visionary changes 21.3, blissful state 32.4, insightfulness 19.4, changed meaning of percepts 13.1, experience of unity 17.9 and disembodiment 10.8.

Closeness to others (area under the curve, mean ± SEM): MDA 168.0 ± 53 against its placebo 11.5 ± 38 (MDA > placebo); MDMA 114.4 ± 44 against its placebo −12.5 ± 16 (MDMA > placebo); MDA and MDMA not significantly different; effect of condition F(3,21) = 5.26, p = 0.0073 (printed in a column headed 'Effect of Condition on Emax', although the values are areas). Insightful and new meanings were raised by MDA and did not differ from MDMA. On the interpersonal adjective scale only MDMA increased Affiliation; no statistic is printed, and the text cites Figure 2 for the figure labelled Figure 3.

Main effects of condition on baseline-corrected maximum heart rate (F(3,22) = 17.1), diastolic (32.4) and systolic blood pressure (61.7), all p < 0.0001. Heart rate rose 20 ± 3 bpm after MDA, significantly less than the 30.6 ± 4.5 bpm rise after MDMA (p = 0.03); peak systolic pressure rose 33 ± 2 mmHg after MDA and 31 ± 3 after MDMA; diastolic 24 ± 2 against 19 ± 2 mmHg, a non-significant trend (p = 0.06). Compared with placebo, prolactin rose 16 ± 6 against 29 ± 6 ng/mL (non-significant trend for MDMA higher, p = 0.07) and cortisol 16 ± 1 against 13 ± 2 µg/dL.

The authors describe MDA as overall similar to MDMA (for example in raising closeness to others) but with fewer dysphoric effects (lower anxiety and impaired control and cognition), and, qualitatively, as appearing to produce a more introverted and emotionally intense prosocial state, against the more extraverted, gregarious one that MDMA seemed to encourage; this is offered as an impression, with no statistic cited for it.

MDA and placebo were given on consecutive days, so half the participants had placebo after MDA; MDA and its metabolite were still detectable on the second day; models of placebo sessions only (physiological, endocrine and visual analogue measures) did not suggest significant sequence effects. Limitations stated by the authors: residual next-day MDA may have altered placebo measures in half the participants; comparison with MDMA data from separate studies reduced power; racemic forms only; and a modest sample, a low number of women and single dose levels, which they say prevent full characterization of MDA's pharmacokinetics.

MDA elimination half-life 10.9 ± 4 h (mean ± SD; the number analysed is not stated; 12 took part). The MDMA kinetics compared in the discussion are from a separate study, Kolbrich et al. (2008a; 1.6 mg/kg oral MDMA; half-life 8.1 ± 2 h), whose authors include Huestis, an author of this paper, not from the MDMA comparison volunteers. The abstract says the similarity of the two drugs' kinetics points to pharmacodynamics, not kinetics, as the reason for MDA's longer effects; the discussion says the difference in duration may be due to the difference in half-life, or to partly different mechanisms.

evidence_set: Both drugs raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature and pupil size compared with placebo; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature significantly more than LSD and psilocybin 15 mg; both LSD doses raised heart rate more than both psilocybin doses and placebo; psilocybin 30 mg, not 15 mg, moderately raised heart rate against placebo. Approximate values of the group mean curves in Fig. 3 (editors' reading, not the per-person maxima analysed; peak values and statistics are in Supplementary Table S5, not read): highest systolic about 139 mmHg (psilocybin 30 mg), 134–135 (15 mg), 131–133 (LSD), with placebo about 118–120 over the same hours; heart rate about 81–82 bpm (LSD 200 µg), 76–77 (LSD 100 µg), 72 (psilocybin 30 mg) and 67–68 (15 mg, at 2–2.5 h), with placebo about 62–65 over the same hours; the 15 mg and placebo curves also have an early point at 0.5 h of about 71–72 and 69–70 bpm; temperature highest about 37.65 °C (psilocybin 30 mg) and 37.3–37.4 (other active conditions), with placebo about 36.7 over the same hours.

Total acute (0–12 h) List of Complaints scores rose with both doses of both drugs against placebo, and subacute (12–24 h) scores with LSD 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg. Adverse events in the evening or within 48 h, by drug (numbers of people): headache 4 after psilocybin and 3 after LSD; migraine 1 (LSD); nosebleed 1 (psilocybin); low mood 2 and 2; nausea 2 (psilocybin) and 1 (LSD); nightmares 1 (psilocybin); restlessness 1 and 1; vivid dreams 1 (LSD); insomnia 1 (psilocybin); involuntary leg movements 1 (LSD). Nine flashback episodes in five people within 72 h (five after LSD, four after psilocybin; a parenthesis says one to 20 times, not explained). No severe adverse events.

After the sessions: psilocybin 15 mg named correctly in 64% of sessions (taken for LSD 100 µg in 29%); psilocybin 30 mg in 57% (taken for psilocybin 15 mg in 29%); LSD 100 µg in 57% (taken for LSD 200 µg in 21%); LSD 200 µg in 61% (taken for LSD 100 µg and for psilocybin 30 mg in 18% each). Placebo was correctly identified in 96% of sessions (a sentence that follows the end-of-study results and names no time point). The text says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, and the discussion that the study was well blinded. Editors' calculation (correct guesses plus guesses of the other dose of the same drug): the right drug was named in at least 64%, 86%, 78% and 79% of sessions.

The authors state a dose equivalence between the two drugs that involves doses not given in this study, reasoning partly from a separate study of psilocybin by the same group; those figures are not recorded here. The analysed LSD content was 11–14% lower than in their earlier studies with the same formulation. Limitations they state: a highly controlled setting and healthy subjects only, so people in other environments and patients with psychiatric disorders may respond differently.

evidence_set: Digit symbol substitution, mean peak differences against placebo: alcohol −5.89 total and −9.0 correct responses, combination −4.89 and −8.11; peak correct responses: alcohol vs placebo and combination vs placebo p < 0.01, alcohol vs combination not significant. Over 6 h (area) alcohol differed from placebo (p < 0.01) and the combination did not. Against placebo the impairment lasted 2–3 h with alcohol (from 1 h to 3–4 h after administration) and 1 h with the combination (1–2 h). Reaction decision time at peak: combination vs placebo p < 0.05, the only significant pair; in the time course both alcohol conditions lengthened total and decision reaction time at some time points, the combination for half an hour (1–1.5 h after MDMA). The same sentence of the text says no differences were observed between the two alcohol conditions but that impairment was greater under the combination; Table 1 shows alcohol vs combination not significant.

The authors say the combination produced a DSST impairment similar to alcohol alone and slightly increased decision time compared with alcohol alone, and that extrapolation to driving is limited; they say the kinetic changes, although statistically significant, are mild in magnitude and could be considered within the range of differences between individuals. They describe a dissociation between subjective and objective sedation, in which people may feel less sedated and feel they perform more efficiently while psychomotor performance stays impaired; they call its road-safety impact unknown and speculate that combined use may potentiate reckless behaviour among drivers. Nobody drove and no rating of one's own performance was taken (the nearest self-rating is the ARCI benzedrine-group scale of intellectual efficiency and energy, which the combination raised above alcohol alone); they say road-safety relevance needs confirmation in field and real-driving studies.

evidence_set: The authors attribute the higher LSD exposure to inhibition of the drug-metabolizing enzyme CYP2D6 by MDMA, citing other studies (the discussion says it could be explained this way; the conclusion calls MDMA a blocker of LSD's metabolism); the enzyme was not measured here. They report no indication of greater serotonin toxicity with the combination and say MDMA did not increase LSD's effect on body temperature. Limitations they state: only one dose of LSD and of MDMA; a highly controlled hospital setting; healthy volunteers only, so people in other environments and patients with psychiatric disorders may respond differently; and outcome measures that may not capture all aspects of the experience or very subtle differences between the combination and LSD alone.
